# Aliasing & the Nyquist Folding Receiver

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem — and how a *modulated* sample clock turns aliasing from a hazard into a wideband-receiver architecture.
**Chapter:** [1 — Data Initialization](../chap1.qmd)

---

## Background

Sampling converts a continuous signal into a discrete sequence. The **Nyquist theorem** says perfect reconstruction is possible only if the sampling rate exceeds twice the highest frequency, $f_s > 2f_\text{max}$. Violate it and high frequencies **fold back** to lower ones — **aliasing**. A sinusoid at $f_0$ sampled at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at

$$
f_\text{alias} = \left| \left( f_0 + \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right) \bmod f_s - \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right|.
$$

For $f_0 = 1.2$ kHz and $f_s = 1$ kHz the spectrum reports **200 Hz**, though the signal was at 1.2 kHz:

<div class="gallery-result">
![A 1.2 kHz tone sampled at 1 kHz appears at 200 Hz; at 3 kHz it is correct](../Figure/figure_aliasing.png)
</div>

But the deeper problem is **ambiguity**: a baseband tone at 200 Hz could equally have come from 1.2 kHz, 2.2 kHz, 3.2 kHz … — any **Nyquist zone** $n$ folds to the same place. Undersample a wide band and you cannot tell where a signal really was. Usually we forbid this with an anti-aliasing filter. The **Nyquist Folding Receiver (NYFR)** does the opposite — it *embraces* the folding and adds one trick to undo the ambiguity.

## Key idea — tag each zone with a modulated clock

A wideband receiver wants to watch many GHz but can only afford a slow ADC. The NYFR deliberately **undersamples** the whole band so every Nyquist zone folds down onto the first — and drives the sample-and-hold with a **phase-modulated clock** instead of a uniform one. If the sampling instants carry a small sinusoidal jitter $\delta t(k) = A_j \sin(2\pi f_m k / f_s)$, a tone at RF frequency $f_\text{RF}$ picks up an induced phase

$$
\phi(k) = 2\pi f_\text{RF}\,\delta t(k) = \underbrace{2\pi f_\text{RF} A_j}_{\text{FM index}}\,\sin\!\left(2\pi \tfrac{f_m}{f_s} k\right).
$$

The tone still lands at its baseband alias, but now wearing an **induced FM whose depth is proportional to $f_\text{RF}$** — i.e. to the Nyquist zone. Read the FM depth off a spectrogram and you recover which zone the signal came from, and hence its true frequency. One slow ADC, the whole band, ambiguity resolved.

## Code

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

fs = 1.0                                   # normalised sample rate (freqs in units of fs)
N, k = 6000, np.arange(6000)
fm, Aj = 0.0005, 8.0                       # clock-modulation frequency and jitter amplitude

# three tones in Nyquist zones 1, 3, 5 — all fold to distinct baseband aliases
tones = [(0.10, 1), (1.25, 3), (2.40, 5)]  # (f_RF in units of fs, zone)

t_uniform = k / fs                                     # ordinary clock  -> plain aliasing
t_nyfr    = k / fs + Aj*np.sin(2*np.pi*fm*k/fs)        # modulated clock -> zone tagging
mix = lambda t: sum(np.cos(2*np.pi*f*t) for f, _ in tones)

f, tt, S = signal.spectrogram(mix(t_nyfr), fs=fs, nperseg=128, noverlap=120, window='hann')
# in S, each tone sits at its alias with a sinusoidal FM of depth 2*pi*f_RF*Aj*fm  ∝  zone
```

## Result

<div class="gallery-result">
![Nyquist Folding Receiver. (a) With a uniform clock, three tones from Nyquist zones 1, 3, 5 fold to flat baseband lines — you cannot tell which zone each came from. (b) With the modulated clock, the same three lines acquire a sinusoidal FM whose depth grows with the true RF frequency: zone 1 stays flat, zone 3 wiggles moderately, zone 5 swings widely — so the zone, and the real frequency, are recovered.](../Figure/figure_nyfr.png)
</div>

Both panels show the same three tones landing at baseband aliases **0.10, 0.25, 0.40 $f_s$**. Under a uniform clock (a) they are flat lines — a 0.40 $f_s$ line could be a zone-1 tone at 0.40 $f_s$, a zone-3 tone at 1.60 $f_s$, a zone-5 tone at 2.40 $f_s$, and so on; nothing distinguishes them. The modulated clock (b) breaks the tie: because the induced FM depth is $\propto f_\text{RF}$, the zone-5 tone swings roughly 24× wider than the zone-1 tone. Measuring that swing recovers the Nyquist zone and reconstructs the true RF frequency — the principle behind analog-to-information receivers that cover many GHz of spectrum with a single modest ADC.

The lesson cuts both ways: aliasing is a hazard you normally filter out *before* sampling — but understood precisely, the same folding can be engineered into a feature.
